🤔 Can reinforcement learning teach diffusion models how every denoising step should improve, instead of only rewarding the final generated image?

𝗗𝗶𝗳𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗢𝗣𝗦𝗗: 𝗢𝗻-𝗣𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰𝘆 𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗗𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝗻 𝗗𝗶𝗳𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀

Recent diffusion RL methods optimize image-level rewards, yet diffusion models generate images through hundreds of intermediate denoising predictions. This creates a fundamental supervision gap:

How can endpoint rewards effectively guide intermediate denoising steps?

In 𝗗𝗶𝗳𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗢𝗣𝗦𝗗, we introduce On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), a new diffusion post-training paradigm that converts image-level reward guidance into explicit intermediate supervision. Reward-guided targets are constructed at sampled denoising queries and continuously refreshed as the policy evolves.

More importantly, we show that target construction and finite optimization are fundamentally different problems—a target with higher reward improvement does not necessarily produce a better optimization update. This suggests a new evaluation principle for diffusion RL.

Across SD3.5-M and Z-Image-Turbo, 𝗗𝗶𝗳𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗢𝗣𝗦𝗗 achieves the best held-out performance in 19/20 reward-matched settings, improves over the strongest baseline by up to 44%, and reduces training GPU-hours by 40–63% compared with DiffusionNFT.

We hope this work provides a new perspective on making diffusion post-training both more effective and more interpretable.

Feedback and discussions are very welcome!

Think about how humans learn a new skill.

You don’t become good at something by reading about it once.

You practice.
You make mistakes.
You try again.
You repeat the same task in different ways until your brain starts to understand what to do.

Robots need that same kind of experience.

The problem is, teaching a robot how to perform real world tasks requires A LOT of training data  and collecting that data in labs is slow, expensive and difficult to scale.

This is where @axisrobotics comes in.

Instead of keeping robot training inside expensive labs, Axis lets ordinary people contribute to the process.

And you contribute to the process by:

→ Open a website and control a virtual robot with your keyboard or mouse

→ Perform simple tasks like picking up and arranging objects

→ And your actions become training data that can help real robots learn.

They’re also using phones to capture real human movements and building tools that can automatically generate thousands of different scenarios for robots to practice.

And honestly, this is the part I find interesting.

Axis is basically turning human experience into robot experience.

Every small movement we make like picking something up, moving it, arranging it, reaching for something can become another example a robot learns from.

It’s almost like giving robots the opportunity to learn from millions of people instead of relying on a handful of robotics labs.

That’s the bigger idea behind Axis.

Robot intelligence shouldn’t be built by a few people in a lab.

It can be built from the everyday actions and experiences of people everywhere.

And Axis is building the data engine to make that possible.
